homophones.sentence: The cyclist squeezed the ___ to slow down at the corner.
homophones.why: A "brake" stops a moving thing; to "break" is to shatter or damage.

homophones.sentence: If the knot is too ___, the rope will slip apart.

homophones.sentence: The express train ___ the station without stopping.
homophones.why: "Passed" is the past tense of the verb "pass," while "past" refers to earlier time or a position beyond something.

homophones.sentence: The ___ spoke to every class during the morning assembly.

homophones.why: "Aloud" means out loud, while "allowed" means permitted.

passages.text: Honeybees do more than make honey. As they move from flower to flower collecting nectar, pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies and rubs off on the next blossom. That accidental delivery service pollinates roughly one out of every three bites of food people eat. When bee populations fall, farmers notice it in their harvests long before shoppers notice it in stores.

passages.text: For centuries, sailors navigated by the stars. A skilled navigator could fix a ship's position using only a sextant, a clock, and a clear night sky. Instruments fail, batteries die, and signals can be jammed — the stars cannot be switched off.

passages.text: Each year a tree adds a new layer of wood beneath its bark, and those layers show up as rings in a cut trunk. passages.text: Mangrove trees grow in salty water along tropical coasts, standing on tangled roots that arch above the surface. Those roots slow incoming waves and trap mud and sand, so the shoreline behind them erodes far more slowly during storms. The same tangle shelters young fish until they are big enough for open water. Coastal towns that cleared their mangroves for docks and shrimp ponds have since spent millions building seawalls to do the same job.

passages.text: No single monarch butterfly makes the whole round trip. passages.text: Scribes in ancient Mesopotamia wrote by pressing a cut reed into damp clay, leaving wedge-shaped marks. Most tablets were meant to be temporary: receipts, school exercises, letters about grain. Then fires swept through storerooms and baked the clay as hard as pottery. Paper and papyrus from the same centuries rotted away, but hundreds of thousands of tablets survived, and much of what we know about Mesopotamian daily life comes from records nobody meant to keep.
passages.mainIdea: Clay records meant to be thrown away lasted by accident and became our main source on Mesopotamian life.
wrong: Mesopotamian writers pressed wedge-shaped marks into damp clay.
Fire can harden soft clay until it is as tough as pottery.
Ancient people kept careful written records of their business.

vocab.meaning: meant to last only a short time

vocabHard.meaning: people whose job was writing things down

clue.answer: wrote by pressing a cut reed into damp clay
wrong: Then fires swept through storerooms and baked the clay as hard as pottery.
records nobody meant to keep

detail.question: Why did so many clay tablets last thousands of years?
detail.answer: Fires in the storerooms baked the clay until it was as hard as pottery.
wrong: Tablets held receipts, school exercises, and letters about grain.
Writers used a cut reed to press marks into the clay.
Paper from the same centuries rotted away.

purpose.answer: to explain how throwaway everyday records turned into lasting evidence
wrong: to teach readers how to read wedge-shaped writing
to describe the steps in firing clay pottery
to argue that ancient schools worked students too hard

inference.answer: Societies that wrote on materials that decay left behind less for us to study.
wrong: Mesopotamian writers expected their notes to last for thousands of years.
Every clay tablet ever made has now been dug up and read.
The storeroom fires destroyed most Mesopotamian writing.

passages.text: A high, fast river of wind called the jet stream snakes west to east across the northern half of the globe. Airliners flying from Los Angeles to New York climb into it and ride along, sometimes gaining a hundred miles an hour over the ground. The return trip fights the same wind, so pilots steer around its cores, the narrow bands where the air moves fastest. That is why an eastbound flight can land an hour before the same route flown west.
passages.mainIdea: The jet stream blows west to east, so it speeds eastbound flights and slows westbound ones.
wrong: The jet stream can add a hundred miles an hour to a plane's speed.
Pilots steer around the fastest bands of the jet stream.
Weather has a large effect on air travel.

vocabHard.meaning: the narrow parts where the wind is strongest
distractors: the engines that power a plane
the inner rock of the earth

clue.answer: the narrow bands where the air moves fastest
wrong: A high, fast river of wind called the jet stream
Airliners flying from Los Angeles to New York climb into it

detail.question: Why can an eastbound flight arrive earlier than the same flight heading west?
detail.answer: The jet stream blows from west to east, pushing eastbound planes along.
wrong: Pilots steer around the fastest bands of wind.
The jet stream sits high above the northern half of the globe.
Airliners have to climb to reach the jet stream.

purpose.answer: to explain how a band of high-altitude wind changes flight times
wrong: to describe how a jet engine produces thrust
to warn readers that westbound flights are unsafe
to compare air travel with travel by train

inference.answer: A pilot flying west may plan a route that stays out of the jet stream.
wrong: The jet stream reverses direction with each change of season.
Airliners cannot climb high enough to enter the jet stream.
Flights from New York to Los Angeles are canceled on windy days.

passages.text: A canal cannot run uphill, so builders break the route into steps called locks. A boat enters a chamber, gates close behind it, and valves let water flow in from the higher stretch until the boat rises with it. Then the front gates swing open and the boat sails out at the new level. No pumps are needed on most canals; gravity moves every gallon, and the boat simply floats on top.
passages.mainIdea: Locks let boats move between water levels on a canal, and gravity does the lifting.
wrong: Gates and valves control the water inside a lock chamber.
A canal cannot be built to run uphill.
Engineers have invented clever ways to move goods by water.

distractors: a rope used to tow boats
a gate at the end of a canal
the act of pulling something longer

vocabHard.meaning: chambers that raise or lower boats between water levels
distractors: fasteners that hold a door shut

clue.answer: valves let water flow in from the higher stretch until the boat rises with it
wrong: A canal cannot run uphill

detail.question: How does a boat rise inside a lock?
detail.answer: Water flows in from the higher stretch and lifts the boat with it.
wrong: The gates in front swing open after the water level changes.

purpose.answer: to explain how a boat moves from one water level to another on a canal
wrong: to describe how workers dig a canal
to argue that canals move goods better than roads do
to compare canals with natural rivers

inference.answer: A lock on most canals would still work during a power outage.
wrong: Boats must be pulled through locks by machines.
A canal carries boats in only one direction.
A lock chamber fills in just a few seconds.

are having

were

are wearing
wearing

subjectVerbAgreement.s: One of my cousins ___ in Arizona.
wrong: live
are living
living

subjectVerbAgreement.s: The flock of geese ___ over the pond every October.
wrong: fly
are flying
have flown

subjectVerbAgreement.s: Both of the windows ___ painted shut.
wrong: is
was
be
subjectVerbAgreement.why: "Both" always refers to two things, so it needs a plural verb.

subjectVerbAgreement.s: The band ___ new uniforms this year.
wrong: have
are having
having

subjectVerbAgreement.s: Somebody in the back rows ___ humming.

were

subjectVerbAgreement.s: Few of the seats ___ empty at the concert.
wrong: was
is
has been

wrong: have
were
are

punctuation.s: After the storm passed ___ we walked down to the beach.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: A comma follows an introductory clause.

punctuation.s: We packed sandwiches ___ apples, and water.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: Commas separate items in a series.

punctuation.s: Bring these items ___ a tent, a lantern, and rope.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence.

punctuation.s: The game was canceled ___ the field was flooded.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses.

punctuation.s: My brother ___ who lives in Austin ___ is visiting in June.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: Commas set off a nonessential clause.

punctuation.s: Maya finished her essay ___ but she forgot to print it.
wrong: no punctuation

punctuation.s: Please hand me the wrench ___ Dad.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: A name used to address someone directly is set off from the rest of the sentence.

punctuation.s: We moved to Denver ___ Colorado, in March.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: A comma separates the name of a city from the state that follows it.

punctuation.s: Did you remember to feed the fish ___
punctuation.why: A sentence that asks something directly ends with an end mark showing inquiry.

punctuation.s: The teacher collected every student___s notebook.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: Ownership by a single person is shown by adding an apostrophe plus s.

punctuation.s: She carried a ten___pound bag of flour up the stairs.
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: Two words acting as one adjective before a noun are joined with a hyphen.

punctuation.s: Lena said ___ "I'll meet you at the corner."
wrong: no punctuation
punctuation.why: A comma separates a speech tag from the quoted words that follow it.

punctuation.s: The tour stops in Lima, Peru ___ Quito, Ecuador; and Bogotá, Colombia.
wrong: no punctuation

punctuation.s: The book on the shelf ___ belongs to Nina.
punctuation.why: Nothing should separate a subject from its verb, even when a phrase describes the subject.

punctuation.s: Swim practice starts at 4___30 tomorrow morning.
punctuation.why: Hours and minutes are divided by a colon when writing a time.

capitalization.why: Sentences start with a capital, and "Paris" is a proper noun.

capitalization.wrong: dr. patel teaches biology at north high school.
capitalization.right: Dr. Patel teaches biology at North High School.
capitalization.why: Titles, names, and school names are proper nouns; subjects like biology are not.
Names of specific places are capitalized; directions are not.

capitalization.wrong: she reads the new york times on mondays.
capitalization.right: She reads The New York Times on Mondays.
capitalization.why: Titles of publications and days of the week are capitalized.
accept: She reads the New York Times on Mondays.

capitalization.wrong: on thanksgiving we drive to aunt rosa's house.
capitalization.right: On Thanksgiving we drive to Aunt Rosa's house.
capitalization.why: Holiday names are proper nouns, and a family title counts as part of the name when it sits in front of one.

capitalization.wrong: my brother and i study spanish on tuesdays.
capitalization.right: My brother and I study Spanish on Tuesdays.
capitalization.why: The pronoun "I" is always capitalized, and so are language names and days of the week.

capitalization.wrong: the pacific ocean is deeper than the caribbean sea.
capitalization.right: The Pacific Ocean is deeper than the Caribbean Sea.
capitalization.why: The full name of a specific body of water is a proper noun, including the word "Ocean" or "Sea" in that name.

capitalization.wrong: we toured the lincoln memorial in washington, d.c., last spring.
capitalization.right: We toured the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., last spring.
capitalization.why: Monuments and cities have proper names, but seasons of the year do not.
accept: We toured the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC, last spring.

capitalization.wrong: our class built a model of jupiter out of clay.
capitalization.right: Our class built a model of Jupiter out of clay.
capitalization.why: Planets have proper names, while ordinary nouns like materials and objects stay lower case.

capitalization.wrong: ms. alvarez read charlotte's web to us after lunch.
capitalization.right: Ms. Alvarez read Charlotte's Web to us after lunch.
capitalization.why: A title used before a person's name is capitalized, and so are the main words in a book title.

capitalization.wrong: the bakery on elm street sells italian bread.
capitalization.right: The bakery on Elm Street sells Italian bread.
capitalization.why: Street names and adjectives made from country names are capitalized, but a general noun like bakery is not.

capitalization.wrong: we read about the boston tea party in history class.
capitalization.right: We read about the Boston Tea Party in history class.
capitalization.why: Named historical events are proper nouns, while ordinary school subjects stay lower case.

capitalization.wrong: the coach said, "practice starts at six."
capitalization.right: The coach said, "Practice starts at six."
capitalization.why: The first word of a complete quoted sentence begins a new sentence and needs a capital.

capitalization.wrong: yellowstone national park is mostly in wyoming.
capitalization.right: Yellowstone National Park is mostly in Wyoming.
capitalization.why: The official name of a park is a proper noun, as is the name of a state.

sentenceType.s: Running through the empty parking lot.
sentenceType.why: There is no subject performing the action — it cannot stand alone.

sentenceType.s: The bell rang and everyone left the classroom quickly.
sentenceType.why: It has a subject and a verb and expresses a full thought.

sentenceType.s: I finished my homework I went outside to play.
sentenceType.why: Two complete sentences are joined with no punctuation or conjunction.

sentenceType.s: Because the road was closed for repairs.
sentenceType.why: A subordinate clause on its own is a fragment.

sentenceType.s: She studied all week, and she passed the exam.
sentenceType.why: Two clauses are joined correctly with a comma and "and".

sentenceType.s: The rain stopped the sun came out the birds returned.
sentenceType.why: Three sentences are strung together without punctuation.

sentenceType.s: The museum opens at nine every Saturday morning.
sentenceType.why: A subject paired with a verb that tells what it does forms a whole thought.

sentenceType.s: A box of old photographs at the top of the closet.
sentenceType.why: A naming phrase needs a verb before it can stand on its own.

sentenceType.s: The library closes early today we should return the books now.
sentenceType.why: Two independent clauses must be separated by end punctuation, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word.

sentenceType.s: To finish the model airplane before Friday.
sentenceType.why: A phrase beginning with "to" plus a verb names an action but never serves as the main verb of a thought.

sentenceType.s: Miguel checked the recipe twice before he turned on the oven.
sentenceType.why: A dependent clause attached to a main clause still leaves a full thought standing.

sentenceType.s: Ana fed the goats, she filled the water trough next.
sentenceType.why: A comma alone is too weak to join two groups of words that could each be a sentence.

sentenceType.s: Which my grandmother planted long before I was born.
sentenceType.why: A clause opening with a relative word like "which" has to describe something in a larger sentence.

sentenceType.s: Volcanoes erupt when pressure builds under the crust.
sentenceType.why: The main clause carries a subject and a verb, so the added time clause only gives extra detail.

sentenceType.s: My front tire went flat I patched it with a repair kit.
sentenceType.why: Two statements crashing together with no punctuation between them make the reader guess where one ends.

sentenceType.s: The wind blew hard, but the tent stayed up.
sentenceType.why: A comma placed before a joining word such as "but" correctly links two equal clauses.

figurativeLanguage.s: The classroom was a beehive during the science fair.
figurativeLanguage.why: The comparison is made by calling one thing the other outright.

figurativeLanguage.s: His hands were as cold as river stones.
figurativeLanguage.why: The comparison is signaled by the word "as".
